outputs.final_proof:
\begin{proof}
Let $G$ be a group of order $pq$, with $p$ and $q$ prime.

If $p=q$, then $|G|=p^2$. Every group of order $p^2$ is abelian, so a subgroup of order $p$ is normal. It is nontrivial and proper, and thus $G$ is not simple.

Suppose instead that $p\ne q$. Relabel the primes so that $p<q$. For the number $n_q$ of Sylow $q$-subgroups, Sylow's theorems give
\[
 n_q\mid p \quad\text{and}\quad n_q\equiv1\pmod q.
\]
Therefore $n_q$ is either $1$ or $p$. Since $p<q$, the equality $n_q=p$ would give $p\equiv1\pmod q$, which is impossible. Hence $n_q=1$. The unique subgroup of order $q$ is normal in $G$ and is neither trivial nor all of $G$. Thus $G$ has a nontrivial proper normal subgroup, so it is not simple.
\end{proof}
